title: Severe and Moderate Asthma Exacerbations in Asthmatic Children and Exposure to Ambient Air Pollutants.
ehr_evidence: We studied asthmatic children born between 1 April 1996 and 31 March 2011 in the province of Quebec (Canada) and identified from a population open birth cohort created with the Quebec Integrated Chronic Disease Surveillance System (QICDSS).
summary: In a population-based cohort of asthmatic children in Quebec, Canada, time-dependent and birth exposure to ambient air pollutants (O3, NO2, PM2.5) was associated with severe asthma exacerbations (hospitalizations or emergency room visits).
key_findings: Time-dependent exposure to NO2 (IQR 4.95 ppb) was positively associated with asthma exacerbation (HR 1.095, 95% CI 1.058–1.131).
Time-dependent exposure to O3 (IQR 3.85 ppb) was positively associated with asthma exacerbation (HR 1.052, 95% CI 1.037–1.066).
Time-dependent exposure to PM2.5 (IQR 1.82 µg/m3) was positively associated with asthma exacerbation (HR 1.025, 95% CI 1.017–1.031).
No significant association was found between exposure at birth to NO2 or O3 and asthma exacerbation.
Exposure at birth to PM2.5 was positively associated with asthma exacerbation (HR 1.051, 95% CI 1.049–1.053).
A significant effect modification was found between NO2 exposure and sex, with increased exacerbation risk for girls (interaction HR 1.057, 95% CI 1.005–1.112).
captured_features: Asthma exacerbations (hospitalization or emergency room visit with asthma diagnosis)
Annual average O3, NO2, and PM2.5 concentrations assigned to residential postal code
study_design: Cohort (population-based cohort with Cox gap-time models)
population: Asthmatic children under 13 years old in Quebec, Canada, born 1996–2011 (population-based cohort, 162,752 children, 1,020,280 person-years)
exposure_domain: Air pollution (ambient air pollutants: O3, NO2, PM2.5)
limitations: Asthma exacerbations defined by health care service use (hospital admissions and ER visits) rather than medication use or self-reported symptoms, potentially capturing only more severe cases.
Exposure assessed using models rather than individual measurements, with exposure assigned to postal code centroids introducing measurement error.
Individual-level information on socioeconomic status, secondhand smoke, and family history of asthma was unavailable.
Residential exposure based on self-reported addresses updated every four years.
PM2.5 exposure held constant (2001–2006 average) throughout follow-up, limiting assessment of temporal variation.
